strengths: Well-motivated approach addressing the real bottleneck of obtaining verifiable rewards for VLM training without human labels or biased LLM judges
Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple domains (vision-language reasoning, vision-centric tasks, graphs) and model sizes (3B, 7B) with consistent positive results

Valuable empirical insights including the 'Goldilocks principle' (task difficulty must match model capacity) and counter-intuitive finding that simple rotation prediction outperforms contrastive learning for vision-language reasoning
Strong qualitative analysis with attention visualizations and case studies demonstrating improved visual grounding and reduced language bias
Thorough ablation studies on task difficulty, model scaling, and task combinations that provide practical design guidance
Generality beyond vision domain demonstrated through graph learning application
Clear presentation, detailed methodology, and commitment to reproducibility
weaknesses: Fundamental scalability limitation: substantial diminishing returns with model size (7.39% improvement at 3B → 1.13% at 7B on MMBench), with root cause (fixed SSL task difficulty) acknowledged but unresolved
Non-additivity of reward combinations—combining all four SSL tasks underperforms best single task (78.77% vs 80.38%)—without investigation of causes or solutions
Lack of principled framework for task selection across domains: contrastive learning works for ImageNet but fails for vision-language reasoning, requiring empirical evaluation for each application
Limited technical novelty: core contribution is recognizing that SSL targets map to RL rewards and validating empirically; uses existing GRPO without modification

Incomplete analysis of why SSL tasks transfer: explanations like 'anti-commonsense' learning for rotation are somewhat speculative; missing deeper investigation of connection between pretext task properties and downstream performance
No comparison with alternative RL-based or other post-training methods for VLMs; only compares to base model
Missing statistical rigor: no confidence intervals, significance testing, or multiple run reporting; some improvements (1-2%) may not be statistically significant
Insufficient investigation of failure modes, particularly why contrastive learning causes negative transfer on some benchmarks (69.27% on MMBench)
Hyperparameter sensitivity unexplored: KL coefficient fixed at 0.01 across all tasks despite varying difficulty; no ablation on GRPO configuration

strengths: Novel perspective on leveraging SSL tasks as verifiable RL reward signals, elegantly bypassing external verifiers and human preference data
Comprehensive experimental study on 3B models with systematic ablations on task difficulty, model size, and task combinations across multiple benchmarks (MMBench, SEED-Bench, ImageNet)
Substantial improvements on 3B models (7.39% MMBench, 8.94% SEED-Bench) with thoughtful analysis of design principles (Goldilocks principle for difficulty matching)
Strong qualitative analysis with attention map visualizations demonstrating improved visual grounding and reduced language bias
Cross-domain extension to graph learning and detailed reproducibility information with promised code release
weaknesses: Severe and unaddressed scalability failure: 7B model results show only 1.13% average improvement (vs 7.39% for 3B), with graph domain showing 1.45% for 7B (vs 13.79% for 3B). This fundamental limitation means the method provides negligible benefit for production-scale VLMs

Critical missing baseline: No comparison with supervised fine-tuning on SSL tasks or other RL reward formulations. The necessity of GRPO over simpler supervised learning is never established, making it unclear if RL complexity is justified

Task combination failure: Naive combination of multiple SSL rewards underperforms single rewards (78.77% vs 80.38%), limiting scalability. Paper identifies the problem but only offers speculative solutions

Weak generalization claims: Graph extension shows highly dataset-dependent results (Cora 34% vs Products <0.5%). Different SSL tasks are needed at different model scales, undermining claims of a unified principle

Design principles are post-hoc observations rather than predictive frameworks. Paper identifies which tasks work empirically but provides no generalizable guidance for practitioners selecting SSL tasks in new domains
Incomplete mechanistic analysis: Explanations for why SSL tasks improve reasoning are largely qualitative. The 'anti-commonsense' learning theory for rotation is speculative without causal evidence
No statistical significance testing: Missing error bars, standard deviations, and significance tests across random seeds. Computational costs not reported
Methodological gaps: No ablation comparing GRPO to supervised fine-tuning; only tested on Qwen models; ImageNet evaluation uses subset rather than full validation set

strengths: Novel perspective on using SSL tasks as verifiable RL rewards, effectively addressing the lack of scalable reward mechanisms for VLM fine-tuning
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple benchmarks (MMBench, SEED-Bench, ImageNet) and model scales (3B, 7B) with strong results on 3B models (7.39% on MMBench, 8.94% on SEED-Bench)

Systematic and insightful ablation studies revealing the 'Goldilocks principle' of task difficulty-capacity matching and the counter-intuitive finding that contrastive learning (dominant in SSL) underperforms in SSL4RL
Strong qualitative analysis with attention heatmap visualizations and case studies demonstrating improved visual grounding and reduced language bias in model outputs
Demonstrates generality by extending the framework to graph domain, suggesting broad applicability beyond vision
Clear presentation with well-motivated problem formulation, effective figures, and detailed hyperparameters supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Significant diminishing returns with model scale: 7B models show only 1.13% improvement on MMBench vs. 7.39% for 3B, limiting practical applicability to commonly-deployed larger models; attempted fixes (increasing task difficulty) show no improvement

Limited technical novelty: the core contribution is a straightforward reformulation of existing SSL objectives as RL rewards, using established GRPO optimization with standard SSL tasks; the perspective is novel but technical execution is incremental

Critical absence of comparative analysis with alternative RL approaches (RLHF, DPO, other verifier-based methods); only compares against untuned base model, making it impossible to assess the relative merit of SSL rewards vs. alternatives

Insufficient guidance for task selection: different SSL tasks work best for different benchmarks, and non-additive combination of rewards suggests interference between tasks; no principled framework exists for selecting tasks for new domains without extensive experimentation

Limited theoretical understanding: lacks rigorous justification for why SSL tasks should help with vision-language reasoning; the 'anti-commonsense learning' explanation is intuitive but not formally analyzed

strengths: Comprehensive empirical study with thorough ablations across multiple dimensions (data volume, model size, task difficulty, task combinations) that identify useful design principles such as task difficulty-capacity matching and semantic alignment

Sound technical contribution: elegant formalization of SSL tasks as RL rewards requiring no downstream labels, human annotations, or external verifiers—addressing a genuine practical limitation of existing approaches
Extensive evaluation across diverse benchmarks (vision-language reasoning, vision-centric tasks, open-ended generation, graph domain) with robust experimental methodology including oracle comparison
Clear presentation with effective figures, well-motivated narrative, and strong reproducibility support (detailed hyperparameters, training curves, promised code release)
Practical cross-domain validation showing generalization to graph learning tasks, supporting the framework's broader applicability
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty over Jigsaw-R1 [52]: while the comprehensive study and generalization are valuable, the core contribution of using SSL tasks as RL rewards feels incremental; the distinction from prior work could be clearer

Severe scaling limitations undermine practical applicability: 7.39% improvement for 3B models but only 1.36% for 7B models, with the paper offering no solution beyond identifying the 'difficulty-capacity matching' problem

Unresolved task selection problem: different SSL tasks optimize different downstream objectives (contrastive works for ImageNet but harms reasoning), requiring downstream knowledge to select tasks a priori, contradicting claims of generality
Meaningful performance gap to oracle: 3.58 pp gap on MMBench and 3.41 pp on SEED-Bench compared to models trained with perfect downstream supervision suggests a non-trivial ceiling

Speculative mechanistic explanations: the claimed 'anti-commonsense learning' mechanism for rotation prediction lacks rigorous evidence; why rotation specifically outperforms other challenging tasks deserves deeper investigation

No statistical significance testing: given modest improvements especially for 7B models, confidence intervals or significance tests would substantially strengthen claims; all results presented as point estimates
Insufficient exploration of hyperparameter sensitivity: only one GRPO configuration tested despite claims of universality; sensitivity to β, entropy coefficient, and group size would be valuable

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple benchmarks (MMBench, SEED-Bench, ImageNet, graph learning) with extensive ablations on data volume, model size, task difficulty, and robustness
Clear problem motivation and intuitive solution: SSL tasks provide intrinsically verifiable reward signals without external labels or unreliable AI judges
Useful empirical insights about SSL-to-RL transfer differences (e.g., contrastive learning underperforms, position prediction surprisingly effective)
Extensive appendices with detailed results, training curves, case analysis, and promised open-source release supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited novelty: core idea of using SSL as rewards is straightforward reinterpretation; incremental over prior Jigsaw-R1 work with unclear sufficient differentiation

Critical scaling failure: improvements drop from 7-8% on 3B models to only 1-3% on 7B models, with authors acknowledging but not solving underlying ceiling-effect due to fixed SSL task difficulty mismatching model capacity
Modest improvements without statistical rigor: no confidence intervals, significance tests, or multi-run error bars despite 3-5% gains; oracle gap of 3-4% suggests SSL rewards are noisy proxies

Lack of theoretical justification: post-hoc explanations for why certain SSL tasks work (e.g., rotation for VQA) rather than principled analysis; no mechanism explaining when/why SSL improves reasoning

Task combination fails: naive combination of all four SSL rewards (78.77%) underperforms best single task (80.38%), suggesting approach is not robust or composable, with only speculative explanations (conflicting objectives)

Insufficient mechanistic analysis: unclear whether improvements come from dense rewards, exploration, or data diversity; missing supervised fine-tuning baseline; attention visualizations show marginal differences

Missing critical baselines: no direct comparison with Jigsaw-R1, no comparison with other VLM alignment methods, no alternative reward designs; Golden oracle comparison uses different training procedure (60% downstream labels vs. SSL)

Potential data contamination: Full Set experiments use 118K samples from benchmarks used for evaluation, with unclear safeguards against test set overlap; test/train split procedure not fully specified

strengths: Novel and well-motivated framework that elegantly repurposes intrinsically verifiable SSL tasks as RL rewards, addressing a genuine bottleneck in VLM alignment

Strong empirical results with substantial improvements on vision-language reasoning (7.39% MMBench, 8.94% SEED-Bench) and competitive performance vs. oracle baseline despite using zero labeled data

Valuable design insights including counter-intuitive findings (contrastive learning ineffectiveness, position task effectiveness) and clear principles for task design (Goldilocks principle, semantic alignment)
Excellent presentation with detailed appendix, transparent methodology, attention visualization analysis, and planned code/model release for reproducibility
Practical scalability without requiring human annotations, external verifiers, or heuristic judges, with demonstrated generalization to non-vision domains
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: framework straightforwardly maps SSL corruption functions to GRPO rewards using existing components; builds incrementally on Jigsaw-R1 prior work

Severe scalability limitations with performance gains diminishing dramatically from 3B models (7.39%) to 7B models (1.36%), limiting practical applicability to larger models that dominate current landscape

Insufficient mechanistic understanding of why SSL objectives transfer to downstream reasoning—'anti-commonsense learning' explanation is intuitive but not rigorously validated, and causal mechanisms remain unclear
Limited guidance for designing SSL tasks in new domains; only four specific tasks tested; non-additivity of multi-task combinations inadequately explained; systematic task discovery process lacking
Incomplete comparison with related work: missing comparisons with alternative RL alignment approaches, other post-training methods, and alternative baseline models beyond single oracle
